title: the courage not to strike
hookLine: a grieving man raises his stick, and the snake asks why
carry: do no harm — start with your mouth

cards: In the great epic, the Mahabharata, a young man named Ruru is about to be married when his bride, Pramadvara, is bitten by a snake and dies.
He weeps alone in the forest until, the story says, a messenger of the gods offers him a way: give her half of your own life. He does, and she wakes. But the grief has turned into rage.
Ruru swears to kill every snake he meets, and he keeps his word. Then one day he finds an old snake lying in the grass, and he raises his stick. The snake speaks.
I've never harmed you, it says. My kind doesn't even bite. Why strike me?

teach.b: The snake turns out to be a sage under a curse, and before he goes he gives Ruru a line the epic repeats more than once: ahimsa is the highest dharma. Ahimsa. Himsa is harm, violence.
Ahimsa is its opposite: not-harming. Ruru's grief was real. But his stick was about to land on someone who had nothing to do with it.

teach.h: HARM TRAVELS TO WHOEVER IS NEAREST.
teach.b: That's how harm often travels, from a hurt toward whoever is nearest. Ahimsa is the half-second where the stick stays down.
The yoga teacher Patanjali puts not-harming first on his list of restraints, before he teaches anything about posture.
It's a big reason so many Hindu families keep vegetarian kitchens, and why a grandmother carries a spider outside in a cup. It isn't soft, either.
Gandhi, who set this word beside truth at the center of his life, confronted an empire and refused the one weapon everyone expected him to pick up.
Some teachers name three places ahimsa lives: thought, word and deed.
Today's line starts with words, because that's where the stick goes up fastest. The cutting joke. The thing said about someone who isn't in the room.
The sharp reply sent at night to whoever happens to be nearest when you're hurting. And the vow points inward too. A voice in the head that calls a person worthless is himsa as well.

how: In Hindu life ahimsa shows up in vegetarian kitchens, care for animals and restraint in speech, and yoga teachers present it as the first of the restraints in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

games.q: Sam was over and Nani carried a spider out of the kitchen in a cup, very serious about it 😂 Sam asked if that's a religion thing. is it??
o: kind of, yes. it's ahimsa, not harming living things. it's also why a lot of Hindu families don't eat meat.
no, Nani just doesn't like squishing bugs.
it's only a rule for yoga class.
games.why: In the Mahabharata, a harmless snake stops Ruru's stick and teaches him that not-harming is the highest dharma. Nani's cup is the same teaching, ahimsa, and so is the vegetarian kitchen.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: swears to kill every snake he meets
never harmed him, doesn't even bite
puts not-harming first on his list

s: the old snake Ruru meets is the one that bit his bride
it never harmed him. his rage was about to land on whoever was nearest.
ahimsa means never standing up for anything
Gandhi built his public life on it and confronted an empire. he refused one weapon, not the fight.
ahimsa covers how you talk to yourself too
the vow points inward too. a voice in the head calling a person worthless is himsa as well.

games.q: you're Ruru. a snake killed your bride, and you've sworn to kill every snake you see. an old snake lies at your feet and asks why you'd strike it. what does the story teach?
o: strike. a snake is a snake.
lower the stick. this one never harmed you, and not-harming is the highest dharma.
walk away and keep hunting the others.
games.why: the snake turns out to be a sage under a curse, and he teaches Ruru that ahimsa is the highest dharma. the hurt was real; the target was wrong.

practice: Now, find the half-second. Bring back the last time you said something sharp, to someone or about someone. Don't punish yourself; that would be harm too.
Replay it slowly, and this time stop at the moment the stick went up, before the words came out. Feel the push to strike. Let it pass through without acting on it.
Was this person really the one who hurt you? Rest there. If you pray, you can ask for a gentler tongue.

wordCard.voice: Ahimsa. Not-harming, in thought, word and deed. The courage not to strike. Seventeenth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: not-harming. Himsa is harm; ahimsa is its opposite.

carryVoice: Your line: do no harm — start with your mouth. Today, let one sharp sentence go unsaid, and notice what happens to the room. Day seventeen.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Paulomi section: Ruru, Pramadvara and the dundubha)
